document_analysis.title: Address Resolution Protocol
document_analysis.author: David R. Pogson
document_analysis.abstract_summary: Describes how hardware and protocol addresses are translated on local networks, specifically Ethernet.

sections_identified.content: Explains the need for address translation (hardware to protocol), mentions ARP as a name for this process.
Hardware addresses are 48-bit and opaque, while network protocols use shorter addresses like Internet Protocol's 32-bit addresses. This mismatch causes routing issues on local networks.
Compares Ethernet (48-bit) vs DECnet/FDDI (60-bit) and discusses how protocols like CHAOS, Internet, PUP, and DECnet use different address lengths.
Defines the packet structure with fields like ar$hrd, ar$pro, ar$hln, etc. Describes how packets are constructed for requests and replies.
Explains REQUEST vs REPLY opcodes, broadcasting requests, and direct replies.
Describes how a monitor can use ARP to debug other protocols without understanding them by observing hardware/protocol address mappings.
Walks through a scenario where machines X and Y communicate via Internet protocol on Ethernet, showing the request-reply cycle.
Discusses table aging, timeouts for moved hosts, daemon-based timeout mechanisms, and resetting tables manually.

formatting_notes: Document is in plain text with some ASCII art representations of packet structures.
Uses $ sign for field names (e.g., ar$hrd).
